name: Dutasteride
lead: Dutasteride, sold as Avodart among other brands, is an oral prescription medication that blocks 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme family that converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT). DHT is the main androgen behind male pattern hair loss, so people use dutasteride to slow or stop the thinning of the hairline and crown and, in many cases, to thicken the hair they still have, helping preserve the density, hairline and overall head of hair that frame the face.[1][4][33]

It is FDA-approved for symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). For hair loss it is prescribed off-label in most countries, while South Korea (2009), Japan (2015) and Taiwan (2016) have approved it for male androgenetic alopecia.[1][2] Within hair-loss and looksmaxxing communities it is widely described as the stronger sibling of finasteride, because it inhibits all three 5-alpha-reductase isoforms and lowers circulating DHT further, and it appears in oral, topical and mesotherapy-style protocols.[1][3][6][28]

Research on hair loss includes randomised, placebo- and finasteride-controlled trials published in 2006 and 2014, systematic reviews and a 2019 meta-analysis; trials of the drug for prostate conditions, such as the REDUCE and CombAT studies, are far larger.[4][11][12][18][10] Reported adverse effects are chiefly sexual and breast-related, and the drug has a long half-life of roughly four to five weeks, which keeps it in the body for months after the last dose.[1][2][5] The online discussion of dutasteride combines enthusiasm for its efficacy with an active thread of side-effect reports and arguments about post-finasteride-type syndromes.[25][26][29]

chain: Blocks type I, II and III 5-alpha-reductase

Preserves or restores hairline and density
angle.text: Dutasteride is used to hold on to hair and to regrow thinning areas in male pattern hair loss, which keeps the hairline and crown fuller. Because it suppresses DHT more completely than finasteride, people in hair-loss communities treat it as the step-up option, taken orally or, in some protocols, applied topically or delivered by mesotherapy.

paras: Androgenetic alopecia, or pattern hair loss, affects about half of men by age 50 according to Wikipedia, and is typically described as a moderately stressful condition that diminishes body image satisfaction.[33] In the scalp, DHT binds follicle androgen receptors in genetically susceptible areas, shortening the growth phase and shrinking follicles over successive cycles. Dutasteride is used to reduce that DHT signal, with the aim of stopping further miniaturisation and letting thinned hairs recover thickness.[1][4]

A review of oral options notes that clinicians increasingly use dutasteride and oral minoxidil off-label, because finasteride is the only oral drug FDA-approved for male alopecia.[3] The same review places probable efficacy in the order dutasteride, finasteride at a higher dose, oral minoxidil, then finasteride at the labelled hair-loss dose.[3] People in looksmaxxing and hair-loss forums typically describe dutasteride as part of a stack with topical or oral minoxidil, microneedling and sometimes a ketoconazole shampoo, aimed at keeping the hairline intact as a major part of facial framing.[26][28]

Wikipedia states that several studies found dutasteride to induce regrowth more rapidly and to a greater extent than the highest approved dose of finasteride, which it attributes to more complete DHT suppression in follicles.[1] Results usually take several months to appear, and clinical trials of hair counts have run for 24 weeks or longer.[4][11]

The drug is also used off-label for female pattern hair loss, although data in women come largely from small or retrospective studies, and it is not used in women who are or may become pregnant because of the risk of genital abnormalities in a male fetus.[1][13]

Finasteride, the first 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, was patented in 1984 and approved by the FDA in 1992 for BPH, then in 1997 at a lower dose for male pattern hair loss; it blocks mainly the type II isoenzyme.[34] Dutasteride was developed at Glaxo Wellcome (later GlaxoSmithKline) as a dual inhibitor of types I and II, was described in the literature in 1997, and won FDA approval for BPH in November 2001 before launching as Avodart in 2002.[1] Wikipedia gives a patent date of 1996 in its history section but 1993 in its lead, and notes that the sources conflict.[1]

The rationale for the hair-loss work was that scalp follicles express both type I and type II enzymes, so a drug blocking both might suppress scalp DHT more than a type II-selective one.[11] A 2006 randomised study by Olsen and colleagues tested that premise in 416 men aged 21 to 45, comparing several dutasteride doses with finasteride and placebo over 24 weeks; the highest dutasteride dose raised hair counts more than finasteride at 12 and 24 weeks, and scalp and serum DHT fell in a dose-dependent way.[11] The US patent expired in November 2015, after which low-cost generics became available, and India now manufactures and exports more generic dutasteride than any other country.[1]

Hair-loss approvals arrived in East Asia first, in South Korea in 2009, then Japan in 2015 and Taiwan in 2016.[1] In the United States and most of Europe, hair-loss use remains off-label. Wikipedia reports that dutasteride ranked 236th among the most commonly prescribed US drugs in 2023, with more than a million prescriptions.[1]

Dutasteride is a competitive, mechanism-based inhibitor of all three 5-alpha-reductase isoforms, with IC50 values of 3.9 nM for type I and 1.8 nM for type II.[1] Both dutasteride and finasteride lower prostate DHT by roughly 85 to 90 percent, where the type II enzyme predominates, but dutasteride lowers circulating DHT by up to about 98 percent against 65 to 70 percent for finasteride.[1] A 2004 study in men with BPH reported marked DHT suppression with dutasteride.[19]

Inhibitors of the enzyme also block synthesis of neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone, a mechanism that has been proposed to explain rare mood and sexual side effects.[1] A 2018 review cited by Wikipedia found no consistent testosterone rise on starting 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, while the 2006 hair-loss study recorded dose-dependent testosterone increases.[1][11]

Oral bioavailability is about 60 percent and food does not impair absorption. Peak levels occur at 2 to 3 hours after a dose, the drug is about 99 percent protein bound, and it is metabolised by CYP3A4 into three active metabolites.[1] The terminal half-life is about 4 to 5 weeks, steady state takes 5 to 6 months, and the drug can be detected for 4 to 6 months after stopping.[1][3] Finasteride's half-life, by contrast, is only 5 to 8 hours.[1]
Dutasteride is a synthetic 4-azasteroid and an analogue of finasteride in which the tert-butyl amide is replaced by a 2,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl group. Its molecular formula is C27H30F6N2O2.[1]

Hair loss data include two key randomised trials and several reviews. The 2006 study randomised 416 men aged 21 to 45 to several dutasteride doses, finasteride or placebo for 24 weeks; all dutasteride arms outperformed placebo in a dose-dependent manner and the top dose beat finasteride.[11] The 2014 phase III trial randomised 917 men aged 20 to 50 to dutasteride at three doses, finasteride 1 mg or placebo for 24 weeks; at 0.5 mg dutasteride produced a larger hair count (P = .003) and width (P = .004) than finasteride in the target area, and panel-rated frontal growth was also higher (P = .002), with similar adverse-event frequency across groups and a short 24-week duration noted as a limitation.[4]

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis compared dutasteride and finasteride in men, and a 2024 systematic review of nine studies (four randomised trials, one single-arm trial, two prospective and two retrospective cohorts, covering doses from 0.02 to 2.5 mg) reported that all active groups beat placebo and that dutasteride at 0.5 mg and 2.5 mg produced larger hair-count gains than finasteride at 1 mg; its authors noted that evidence for women is very limited and that several trials were small or short.[12][13] An updated 2024 review covers dutasteride for androgenetic alopecia more broadly.[14] A randomised placebo-controlled study tested microneedling combined with topical dutasteride solution.[15] Registered studies include a post-marketing surveillance study of 712 patients with alopecia (NCT01004809) and a bioequivalence study of 0.1 mg capsules (NCT01929330).[16][17]

For the prostate, the REDUCE trial randomised 6,729 men aged 50 to 75 with elevated PSA and a prior negative biopsy to dutasteride or placebo for four years; cancer was found in 659 of 3,305 men on dutasteride and 858 of 3,424 on placebo, a 22.8 percent relative reduction, while twelve Gleason 8 to 10 tumours appeared in years 3 and 4 on dutasteride versus one on placebo, and heart failure was reported in 0.7 percent versus 0.4 percent.[18] Acute urinary retention fell from 6.7 percent to 1.6 percent.[18] A 2002 study of 4,325 men with BPH and the CombAT trial of dutasteride with tamsulosin form the basis of the BPH indication.[8][9][10]

The label lists impotence, decreased libido, ejaculation disorders and breast disorders as the most common reactions.[2] In the largest BPH study of 6,729 men, Wikipedia reports erectile dysfunction in 9 percent (5.7 percent on placebo), decreased libido in 3.3 percent (1.6 percent) and breast enlargement in 1.9 percent (1 percent), with effects lessening over the four years and under 5 percent discontinuing for adverse effects.[1] Semen volume falls by about 30 percent on average in affected men, and these changes reverse 3 to 4 months after stopping, according to the same page.[1]

A 2019 meta-analysis of 15 randomised double-blind trials (4,495 subjects) found a 1.57-fold relative risk of sexual dysfunction with 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors overall, 1.66 for finasteride and a non-significant 1.37 for dutasteride, with limited dutasteride data.[5] A comparison review associates oral finasteride and dutasteride with sexual dysfunction and neuropsychiatric side effects.[3] A 2024 meta-analysis of over 2.2 million patients, cited by Wikipedia, found no causal link between these drugs and neurological effects.[1]

Some men report sexual, mood or depressive symptoms persisting after stopping the drug; Wikipedia describes this as disputed, with open questions about the nocebo effect and self-report reliability.[1][34] On T Nation, users attribute lasting impotence or penile changes to dutasteride, including after topical or short use; these are anecdotes, and no controlled study has examined those outcomes.[21][23][24]

The FDA label states dutasteride reduces serum PSA by about 50 percent, that a confirmed PSA rise may signal prostate cancer, and that the drug may raise the risk of high-grade prostate cancer; Wikipedia notes a warning added in 2011 and says the American Urological Association suggests adjusted screening for men on these drugs.[2][1] Women who are or may be pregnant should not handle the capsules, and donors should not give blood during treatment or for at least six months afterwards.[2][1]

In October 2024 the European Medicines Agency began a review of finasteride and dutasteride over possible links to suicidal ideation. In 2025 it confirmed that suicidal thoughts can occur as a side effect of finasteride, mostly at the 1 mg dose, and, according to Wikipedia, said the evidence did not support a similar link for dutasteride.[34]

sections.h: Use in hair-loss and looksmaxxing communities
paras: Threads on tressless.com and r/tressless ask why dutasteride is not recommended first, compare it with finasteride or ask whether to switch from one to the other; one popular framing calls it the off-label favourite for male pattern baldness.[25][26][27][30] These communities usually treat the hairline as a central element of facial attractiveness and discuss dutasteride alongside minoxidil, microneedling and hair transplants, and sometimes as a way to protect transplant results.[26]

On T Nation, users on testosterone therapy or anabolic steroids discuss topical dutasteride alone or with RU58841 or CB-03-01 to manage hair loss while keeping systemic androgens, and some say topical use avoids the sexual side effects reported with oral drugs, while others report symptoms anyway.[7][28][31] The topical route is the subject of a 2025 review, which describes efforts to develop nanocarrier formulations that target follicles with less systemic uptake and notes that a safe commercial product is hard to develop.[6] Dutasteride is also an ingredient in some mesotherapy preparations, which a published study evaluated in female pattern hair loss.[28]

Finasteride is the related first-generation drug; oral and topical minoxidil, microneedling, platelet-rich plasma, low-level laser devices and hair transplantation are the other tools commonly combined with 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.[3][15][33] Dutasteride is also used in some transgender women's hormone regimens, where it has a limited effect compared with androgen-receptor blockers, and is under investigation for premenstrual dysphoric disorder because it may block conversion of progesterone to allopregnanolone.[1] In prostate research it has been studied with bicalutamide and with tadalafil.[1]

Dutasteride is prescription-only in the United States and United Kingdom.[1] Patent expiry in 2015 made generics widely available.[1] Its use for hair loss is approved in only a few countries and is off-label elsewhere.[1]

lore.intro: In hair-loss communities dutasteride is discussed as the stronger alternative to finasteride, used orally, topically or by mesotherapy, with a parallel thread of side-effect reports and debate over post-finasteride-type syndromes.[25][26][28]

claims.claim: Dutasteride is stronger than finasteride and should be tried first
claims.believers: Posts ask why the community does not recommend it directly and describe it as the off-label favourite for male pattern baldness.[26][30]
claims.experts: A 2014 phase III trial found dutasteride 0.5 mg gave greater hair count and width than finasteride 1 mg over 24 weeks, and a 2024 systematic review reached a similar conclusion, noting small trials and short follow-up.[4][13]

claims.claim: Topical dutasteride avoids the side effects of the oral drug
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said topical dutasteride gave him no sides unlike topical finasteride, though another reported penile shrinkage afterwards.[28][21]
claims.experts: A 2025 review says developing a safe and effective topical product is challenging and aims to limit systemic absorption; a poster notes some topical drug still reaches blood.[6][31]

claims.claim: Dutasteride can cause lasting impotence or hormonal damage
claims.believers: Users describe impotence continuing months after short use, or hard-flaccid symptoms and penile changes.[23][21][24]
claims.experts: A 2019 meta-analysis found a non-significant increase for dutasteride in trials, but with few studies; labels list sexual effects, and the half-life is weeks.[5][2][1]

claims.claim: Dutasteride raises testosterone more than finasteride
claims.believers: A poster states it raises testosterone more and cites a PubMed link.[32]
claims.experts: The 2006 trial recorded dose-dependent testosterone increases, while a 2018 review summarised by Wikipedia found no consistent increase overall.[11][1]

claims.claim: Dutasteride microneedling or mesotherapy enhances results
claims.believers: Users report dutasteride mesotherapy as part of their hair protocol.[28]
claims.experts: A randomised placebo-controlled study of microneedling with topical dutasteride has been published, and a dutasteride-containing mesotherapy study in women with pattern hair loss reported photographic and morphometric outcomes.[15]

claims.claim: Dutasteride's long half-life makes side effects last for months
claims.believers: Users describe symptoms lingering well after stopping, and caution that the drug stays in the system.[23][29]
claims.experts: The label and Wikipedia report a half-life of 4 to 5 weeks and detectability for 4 to 6 months; semen changes reverse within 3 to 4 months of stopping.[1][2]

claims.claim: Dutasteride is more likely than finasteride to cause problems
claims.believers: Posters share anecdotes of dutasteride side effects and cite post-finasteride-style syndromes.[29][22]
claims.experts: The 2019 meta-analysis found sexual dysfunction risk 1.66 for finasteride and a non-significant 1.37 for dutasteride, and the EMA's 2025 review reported no evidence of a suicidality link for dutasteride.[5][34]

claims.claim: Dutasteride is as safe as finasteride for the prostate
claims.believers: Users on 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors treat it as an equivalent drug.[26]
claims.experts: The label notes a roughly 50 percent PSA reduction and a warning on high-grade prostate cancer, and REDUCE reported more Gleason 8 to 10 tumours in years 3 and 4 on dutasteride.[2][18]
